reference.source: Rockwood and Green's Fractures in Adults
clinicalPearls: An intra-articular fracture-dislocation of the base of the first metacarpal, characteristically a two-part injury
A volar-ulnar fragment held by the anterior oblique (beak) ligament remains reduced against the trapezium while the metacarpal shaft subluxes
The abductor pollicis longus pulls the shaft proximally, dorsally and radially, while the adductor pollicis adds an adduction and supination force, causing loss of reduction
The typical mechanism is an axial load along a partially flexed thumb metacarpal
Anatomical restoration of the joint surface is the goal, achieved by closed reduction with percutaneous Kirschner-wire fixation or open reduction and internal fixation
Distinguishing the two-part Bennett from the comminuted Rolando pattern guides fixation strategy
Residual articular incongruity or subluxation predisposes to painful trapeziometacarpal arthritis
reference.pathophysiology: An axial force transmitted along a flexed first metacarpal fractures the volar-ulnar corner of its base. This small volar fragment is anchored to the trapezium by the strong anterior oblique (beak) ligament and therefore stays in place, while the remainder of the metacarpal displaces. The abductor pollicis longus and adductor pollicis then pull the shaft proximally, dorsally, radially and into supination, producing the characteristic subluxation at the trapeziometacarpal joint. Because the injury involves the articular surface of a highly mobile joint, incongruent healing accelerates degenerative change.
additionalDifferentials: Ulnar collateral ligament injury of the thumb (gamekeeper/skier thumb)
additionalInvestigations: Anteroposterior, lateral and oblique thumb radiographs
A dedicated true anteroposterior view of the trapeziometacarpal joint (Robert view)
Assessment of the degree of joint subluxation and articular step
CT to evaluate articular congruity and exclude comminution
Stress views if concurrent ligamentous injury is suspected
redFlags: Articular step-off or incongruity predisposing to early arthritis
Persistent subluxation of the trapeziometacarpal joint after reduction
Comminution reclassifying the injury as a Rolando pattern
Loss of reduction due to unopposed abductor pollicis longus pull
reference.prognosis: Anatomical reduction with stable fixation generally yields good thumb function, whereas residual articular incongruity or subluxation predisposes to early trapeziometacarpal osteoarthritis and pain.
pitfalls: Accepting a non-anatomical reduction of the articular surface
Failing to counter the deforming pull of abductor pollicis longus, allowing loss of reduction
Confusing the injury with a comminuted Rolando pattern
Under-imaging and missing the extent of articular involvement
references: Rockwood and Green's Fractures in Adults
management: Achieve anatomical reduction of the trapeziometacarpal joint surface, the primary goal to prevent post-traumatic arthritis
Stabilise most two-part fractures with closed reduction and percutaneous Kirschner-wire fixation
Use open reduction and internal fixation for larger fragments or where closed reduction fails to restore articular congruity
Provide analgesia with thumb spica immobilisation and elevation in the early period
Distinguish the two-part Bennett from a comminuted Rolando pattern on imaging to guide the fixation strategy
Institute hand therapy and progressive mobilisation after fixation to restore thumb function
Monitor radiographically for maintenance of reduction and surveil for later trapeziometacarpal osteoarthritis
